params.title: Circuits
params.subtitle: Tuned circuits, op-amps, phase-locked loops, synthesizers and mixers, then the exam's schematic figures, step by step.

onScreen: Tuned circuits, op-amps, PLLs, synthesizers and mixers, then the exam's schematics
scenes.narration: Welcome to Circuits. This lesson is about what happens when you connect a radio's simple parts. A tuned circuit picks out one frequency, like one station on a dial. An operational amplifier, or op-amp, makes a weak signal stronger. A phase-locked loop holds a radio exactly on its frequency, a synthesizer builds many exact frequencies from one, and a mixer moves a signal from one frequency to another. Then you'll learn to read the exam's schematic drawings and work out what each circuit does. No background is needed: we'll refresh each basic idea as we go. By the end, you'll be able to answer every question in this subelement, and say why the answer is right. Let's start with the basics.

params.title: Voltage, current and resistance
steps: E: voltage, the push, in volts
I: current, the flow, in amperes
R: resistance, the opposition, in ohms

onScreen: E: voltage, the push, in volts
I: current, the flow, in amperes
scenes.narration: Everything in this lesson rests on 3 ideas, and water in a pipe makes them easy to picture. Voltage is the push, like water pressure. It's measured in volts, and in formulas it often gets the letter E. Current is the flow, like the amount of water moving through the pipe each second. Its unit is the ampere, letter I. Resistance is whatever holds the flow back, like a narrow section of pipe. It's measured in ohms, letter R. Ohm's law ties all 3 together: I equals E over R, current equals voltage divided by resistance. So 10 volts pushing through 5 ohms drives 2 amperes. For the same push, less opposition means more current. One more word: a battery's current flows steadily one way. That's DC, direct current.

params.title: AC, coils and capacitors
items: AC: current that flows back and forth. Cycles per second: the frequency, in hertz
Reactance: how a coil or capacitor opposes AC, in ohms
Coil (inductor): its reactance, X<sub>L</sub>, rises with frequency
Capacitor: blocks DC; its reactance, X<sub>C</sub>, falls as frequency rises
Impedance: resistance and reactance together, in ohms

onScreen: AC: back and forth; frequency in hertz
Reactance: a coil's or capacitor's opposition to AC
Coil: X sub L rises with frequency
Capacitor: blocks DC; X sub C falls with frequency
scenes.narration: Radio circuits, though, mostly carry the other kind: AC, alternating current, which flows forward, then back, over and over. Each back-and-forth is a cycle, and the number of cycles per second is the frequency, in hertz. Coils and capacitors oppose AC by an amount that changes with frequency: that's reactance, also in ohms. A coil of wire, called an inductor, fights any change in its current. The faster the current reverses, the harder it pushes back, so its reactance, X sub L, rises with frequency. A capacitor is 2 metal plates with an insulator between. DC just fills the plates and stops: a capacitor blocks DC. But the faster AC reverses, the less the plates fill and push back, so X sub C falls. Resistance and reactance together make up the total opposition, called impedance.

marks.label: Resonance: X<sub>L</sub> = X<sub>C</sub>
marks.note: In series they cancel: impedance ≈ R

onScreen: Low frequency: X sub C large
High frequency: X sub L large
Resonance: X sub L equals X sub C; in series they cancel, impedance about R
scenes.narration: Put a coil and a capacitor in one circuit, and sweep the frequency upward. At low frequencies, the capacitor's reactance is large; at high frequencies, the coil's is. In between is one frequency where X sub L exactly equals X sub C. That's resonance, and it's how a tuned circuit picks out one frequency. Now connect a resistor, coil and capacitor one after another in a single loop: a series R-L-C circuit, short for resistor, inductor, capacitor. The coil's and capacitor's voltages always push in opposite directions, half a cycle apart: 180 degrees out of phase. We'll see why shortly. At resonance they're equal as well, so they cancel, leaving only the resistance. So the impedance of a series R-L-C circuit at resonance is approximately equal to the circuit resistance: its minimum.

onScreen: X sub L and X sub C cancel
scenes.narration: So the coil and capacitor drop out, and the exam's choices of approximately X sub L or X sub C are wrong: those cancelled. Now apply Ohm's law: current equals the push divided by the opposition. With the impedance at its minimum, the current is at its maximum. Say 10 volts is applied across 5 ohms of resistance: 2 amperes flow, just as if the coil and capacitor weren't there. So the current flow in a series R-L-C circuit at resonance is maximum, and it's simply I equals E over R. Don't pick minimum: that's the opposite. And it isn't zero or DC: the current is still AC, flowing back and forth at the resonant frequency.

blocks.label: Coil L
blocks.note: Large current × X<sub>L</sub>: a big voltage

blocks.label: Capacitor C
blocks.note: Just as big, in opposite phase

onScreen: Across the coil: a big voltage
Across the capacitor: just as big, opposite phase
scenes.narration: Resonance has another surprise: the voltage across the coil can be far bigger than the voltage you apply. Think of a swing. Small pushes, timed to its natural rhythm, build a big swing. In a series circuit at resonance, only the small resistance limits the current, so the current is large. By Ohm's law turned around, the voltage across any part is its current times its opposition. So that large current, flowing through the coil's reactance, develops a big voltage across the coil, and the same across the capacitor. The 2 big voltages are opposite, so they cancel around the loop, and the source only has to supply the small voltage the resistance needs.

params.title: Q, the quality factor
steps: Q: how strong the resonance is
params.answer: Resonance: more than the applied voltage

onScreen: V sub L about Q times the applied voltage
Q: how strong the resonance is
In series: Q = X sub L over R
Resonance: more than the applied voltage
scenes.narration: How big does that voltage get? About Q times the applied voltage, across the coil and again across the capacitor. Q, the quality factor, rates how strong a resonance is. In a series circuit, it's how many times larger the reactance is than the resistance. With a Q of 100, just 1 volt applied gives about 100 volts across the coil. That's the exam's answer: resonance is how the voltage across reactances in series can be greater than the applied voltage. The other choices can't do it: not resistance, not conductance, which is just how easily current flows, and not capacitance alone. It takes a coil and capacitor at resonance.

params.title: Phase: are current and voltage in step?
rows: In phase: they rise and fall together
Current lags by 90°: it builds up late
Current leads by 90°: it flows while filling

scenes.narration: We've used the word phase a few times, so let's pin it down. Phase is about timing: does the current rise and fall at the same moments as the voltage? It's measured in degrees, where half a cycle is 180 degrees and a quarter cycle is 90. In a plain resistor, current and voltage rise and fall together: they're in phase. A coil fights each change, so its current builds up late: it lags the voltage by 90 degrees. A capacitor's current flows hardest while its plates are filling, before the voltage peaks, so it leads by 90 degrees. One is a quarter cycle late, the other a quarter cycle early, so a coil and capacitor always work half a cycle apart.

params.title: At resonance: voltage and current in phase
labels: Power factor 1: all the power does real work

scenes.narration: So what happens at resonance, where the coil and capacitor are equally strong? Their opposite timing effects cancel, just as their reactances did. What's left behaves like a plain resistor: the circuit looks purely resistive. So in a resonant circuit, the voltage and current are in phase, rising and falling together. The power factor, the share of the power doing real work, is then 1: all of it. On the exam, the traps are current leading by 90 degrees, or voltage leading by 90 degrees: those describe a lone capacitor or a lone coil. And 180 degrees out of phase is wrong too.

params.title: Parallel resonance: the tank circuit
items: Resistor, coil and capacitor side by side, each across the source
Coil and capacitor in parallel: a tank circuit
Line current: from the source, split into a branch through each part
At resonance, coil and capacitor branch currents are equal and 180° apart
They cancel in the line: the source only feeds the resistor

onScreen: Parts side by side, each across the source
Coil and capacitor: a tank circuit
Line current splits into the branches
scenes.narration: So far, our parts have been in series. Now arrange the same 3 parts side by side, each connected straight across the source. That's a parallel circuit, and a coil and capacitor in parallel are often called a tank circuit. The current from the source, called the line current, splits into a branch through each part. At resonance, the coil and capacitor have equal reactances and the same voltage across them, so their branch currents are equal. But they're 180 degrees out of phase: while one flows in, the other flows out. So in the line, they cancel. The coil and capacitor together act like an open switch, and the source only has to feed the resistor.

params.title: Parallel resonance: impedance at its maximum

marks.label: X<sub>L</sub> small
marks.note: The coil lets extra current through

marks.label: X<sub>C</sub> small
marks.note: The capacitor lets extra current through

onScreen: Low frequency: the coil passes extra current
High frequency: the capacitor passes extra current
Resonance: impedance about R, its maximum
scenes.narration: Now sweep the frequency, as we did for the series circuit. Below resonance, the coil's reactance is small, so the coil lets extra current through. Above resonance, the capacitor's reactance is small, so it does the same. For the same voltage, more current means less impedance. That's the opposite of the series circuit, where moving away from resonance added opposition. Only at resonance do the branch currents cancel, leaving just the resistor. So the impedance of a parallel R-L-C circuit at resonance is approximately equal to the circuit resistance, and here that's its maximum. Low compared with the resistance is the trap, and so are X sub L and X sub C: their currents cancelled.

params.title: Inside the tank: a circulating current
labels: The coil's field collapses and recharges the capacitor
Circulating current ≈ Q × line current: maximum

onScreen: Circulating current about Q times line current: maximum
scenes.narration: The branch currents cancel in the line, but they haven't vanished: they're circulating inside the tank. Picture the capacitor charged up. It discharges through the coil, and that current builds the coil's magnetic field, which is where a coil stores its energy. When the capacitor is empty, the field collapses and keeps the current going, charging the capacitor back up the other way. Then it all repeats at the resonant frequency, like the swing from before trading height for speed. This circulating current is large: about Q times the line current. So the current flow within the parallel elements at resonance is maximum, while the line current is at its minimum. On the exam, minimum is the trap: that's the line current.

params.title: Series and parallel resonance side by side
rows: Branch currents cancel in the line

onScreen: Impedance about R: series minimum, parallel maximum
Series: reactances cancel; parallel: branch currents cancel
Series current maximum; parallel line current minimum
Both: voltage and current in phase
scenes.narration: Here's the whole picture side by side. In both circuits at resonance, the impedance is approximately equal to the circuit resistance. In series, that's its minimum, because X sub L and X sub C cancel. In parallel, it's its maximum, because the branch currents cancel in the line. So the series current is maximum, I equals E over R, while the parallel line current is minimum. Inside the parts, the series circuit carries that same maximum current through everything, and the parallel tank circulates about Q times the line current. In both, voltage and current are in phase. The takeaway: at resonance the reactances cancel, leaving just the resistance.

params.title: Meet the op-amp
items: Amplifier: a small signal in, a bigger copy out. Gain: how many times bigger
Op-amp, operational amplifier: a chip with 2 inputs and 1 output
Inverting input (−) and non-inverting input (+)
Amplifies the difference between them: a huge open-loop gain
The output can't go past its supply voltages: the rails

onScreen: Inverting input minus, non-inverting input plus
Huge open-loop gain on the difference
Output limited by the supply rails
scenes.narration: Tuned circuits can pick out a frequency, but they can't make a weak signal any stronger. That's the job of an amplifier: a small signal goes in, and a bigger copy comes out. How many times bigger is called the gain. The workhorse is the op-amp, short for operational amplifier: a complete amplifier on one small chip, with 2 inputs and 1 output. One input is marked minus: the inverting input. The other is marked plus: the non-inverting input. It amplifies the difference between their voltages. On its own, with nothing connected from the output back to the inputs, its gain is huge. That's called the open-loop gain. But the output can't swing past the supply voltages that power the chip. Those limits are the supply rails.

params.title: The comparator: an op-amp run open loop
labels: No feedback: the full open-loop gain
Plus input higher: output jumps to the top rail
Minus input higher: output drops to the bottom rail
Tells which input is higher: a comparator

onScreen: Plus input higher: output to the top rail
Minus input higher: output to the bottom rail
A comparator: which input is higher
scenes.narration: Let's start with the simplest way to use an op-amp: just as it is, with nothing feeding the output back to the inputs. That's called open loop, or no feedback. With such a huge gain, even a tiny difference between the inputs drives the output all the way to one supply rail or the other. If the plus input is even slightly higher, the output jumps to the top rail. If the minus input is higher, it drops to the bottom rail. That tells you which input voltage is higher, so this circuit is called a comparator. On the exam, the op-amp circuit operated open-loop is the comparator. The other exam choices, amplifiers and an active filter, all use feedback, as you'll see next.

params.title: Negative feedback: output to the − input

blocks.label: External feedback network
blocks.note: Output back to the inverting input (−)

blocks.label: Output
blocks.note: Pulled back if it swings too far

onScreen: External feedback network: output to the inverting input
Output pulled back if it swings too far
scenes.narration: A comparator is all or nothing. To get a steady, predictable gain instead, we feed part of the output back. An external feedback network, parts outside the chip, often just a resistor or two, connects the output back to the inverting input. That's negative feedback. If the output swings too high, the feedback raises the minus input, and raising the minus input pulls the output back down. It's like cruise control in a car, constantly correcting. So the external feedback network that controls the gain connects from the output to the inverting input. From the output to the non-inverting input would be positive feedback, which reinforces itself instead of correcting. And a network between the inputs wouldn't feed the output back at all.

params.title: What sets a closed-loop gain?
rows: The op-amp balances feedback against input
The chip's own gain is huge and varies
They only limit how far and fast it swings

onScreen: Supply voltage and slew rate: no
scenes.narration: So who decides how much gain a closed-loop circuit, one with feedback, has? Not the chip. An op-amp's own open-loop gain is huge, and it varies from one chip to the next, so nobody relies on it. Negative feedback tames that huge gain: the op-amp simply settles wherever the feedback balances the input, and that balance point depends only on the feedback parts. So the gain of a closed-loop op-amp circuit is determined by the op-amp's external feedback network: the resistors you choose. Not an internal feedback network. And not the supply voltage or the slew rate, the op-amp's speed limit: those only limit how far and how fast the output can swing.

blocks.label: Output
blocks.note: 180° out of phase with the input

blocks.label: R<sub>f</sub>
blocks.note: Feedback: output to the inverting input

onScreen: Input through R sub in to the inverting input
R sub f: feedback, output to the inverting input
scenes.narration: Now the most common closed-loop circuit: the inverting amplifier. The input signal goes in through a resistor, R sub in, to the inverting input. The plus input is grounded: connected to 0 volts. Because the signal drives the minus input, the output moves the opposite way: when the input rises, the output falls. So the input and output signals are 180 degrees out of phase: the output is an upside-down copy. A feedback resistor, R sub f, runs from the output back to the inverting input, and sets the gain. On the exam, in phase and 90 degrees out of phase are the traps.

params.title: Inverting amplifier gain
steps: Minus sign: the output is inverted

onScreen: Gain = minus R sub f over R sub in
R sub f 100 kilohms, R sub in 10 kilohms
scenes.narration: How much gain? It's minus R sub f over R sub in: the feedback resistor divided by the input resistor. The minus sign doesn't mean the signal shrinks; it just marks the inversion. Let's try numbers. Resistor values are often given in kilohms, and a kilohm is 1000 ohms. Say R sub f is 100 kilohms and R sub in is 10 kilohms. 100 divided by 10 is 10, so the gain is minus 10: the output is 10 times bigger than the input, and upside down. Want more gain? Use a bigger feedback resistor. The op-amp itself doesn't change the answer: only the 2 resistors do.

params.title: Audio filters: passive LC or op-amp?
rows: Insertion loss: a little is lost
Gain: it can come out stronger

onScreen: Passive: coils and capacitors; active: op-amp
Op-amp filter needs no bulky coils
scenes.narration: Op-amps also make better filters. A filter lets some frequencies through and holds others back, like a sieve for signals. An audio filter, for sound, might pass a voice and cut out a whine. A passive filter is built only from coils and capacitors, so it's called an LC filter, after their letters, L and C. With no power source of its own, it always loses a little of the signal: that's insertion loss. An active filter uses an op-amp with resistors and capacitors, so it can filter and amplify at once. That's the main advantage of an op-amp audio filter over a passive LC audio filter: op-amps exhibit gain rather than insertion loss. They need no bulky coils, either. Vibration, availability and retooling are the traps.

params.title: Closed loop or open loop?
rows: Gain set by the network, in phase
Output driven to a supply rail

scenes.narration: Let's sort the op-amp circuits the exam names. The inverting amplifier, the non-inverting amplifier, and the active filter are all closed-loop circuits. The non-inverting amplifier is the one that feeds the signal to the plus input, so its output stays in phase. Each has an external feedback network, from the output to the inverting input, and that network sets the gain. The odd one out is the comparator: operated open-loop, with no feedback, so its output slams to a supply rail. The takeaway: feedback to the minus input gives a steady gain, and no feedback gives a comparator.

params.title: Oscillators: timing with R and C
steps: C fills through R, like a bucket through a hose
Bigger C or R: slower filling, longer period
Double the period → half the frequency

onScreen: C fills through R like a bucket through a hose
Bigger C or R: longer period
Double the period, half the frequency
scenes.narration: One more op-amp circuit is on the exam: the oscillator. It makes its own repeating wave, with no input signal, and every radio needs one to make its signals. The time for 1 complete cycle is the period, and the frequency is how many cycles fit into each second. So frequency equals 1 divided by the period. Many oscillators keep time with a capacitor charging through a resistor, like a bucket filling through a hose. A bigger bucket, more capacitance, meaning the capacitor holds more, or a narrower hose, more resistance, takes longer to fill. Longer filling means a longer period, and a lower frequency: double the period, and you halve the frequency. Keep that bucket in mind: you'll need it shortly.

callouts.label: Lines are wires; a dot joins wires
Zigzag: a resistor. 100K means 100 kilohms
2 short parallel lines: a capacitor, C
Triangle: the op-amp, with its − and + inputs
Stacked lines at the far left: ground, the 0-volt return

onScreen: Lines are wires; dots join them
scenes.narration: The exam's oscillator question comes with a drawing, Figure 3D6, so first let's learn to read a schematic. A schematic is a map of the connections, not a picture of the parts. Lines are wires, and a dot means wires are joined. A zigzag is a resistor, and the label 100K means 100 kilohms. 2 short parallel lines are a capacitor, here labeled C. The big triangle is the op-amp, with its minus and plus inputs on the left and its output at the point. And the little stack of lines at the far left is ground: the common return, at 0 volts, that every voltage is measured from.

callouts.label: The output charges C through R, on the − input
The 100K and 10K divider sets a switching point on the + input
C passes that point: the output flips to the other rail
Output: a square wave

onScreen: Divider sets the switching point on the plus input
scenes.narration: Now let's see how Figure 3D6 works. Start with the output sitting at one supply rail. Through resistor R, it slowly charges capacitor C, and C is wired to the minus input. Meanwhile, the 100 kilohm resistor and the 10 kilohm one below it form a divider: 2 resistors in series that split the output voltage, with the point between them feeding a small share to the plus input. That's the positive feedback we set aside earlier, and it sets a switching point. When the capacitor's voltage creeps past that point, the op-amp flips, like a comparator, to the other rail. Then C discharges and charges the other way until the op-amp flips back. Over and over: the output is a square wave, jumping between the 2 rails.

params.title: Figure 3D6: double the capacitance
steps: Double C: it takes twice as long to charge
Twice the charging time → twice the period
Twice the period → half the frequency
The inputs are not reversed: it works as drawn

onScreen: Double C: twice as long to charge
Inputs not reversed: works as drawn
scenes.narration: The exam asks: what if the capacitance of C were suddenly doubled? Go back to the bucket. A bucket twice the size takes twice as long to fill through the same hose, so C takes twice as long to charge through R before each flip. Each cycle then takes twice as long: the period doubles. And since frequency is 1 divided by the period, the frequency halves. Don't be thrown by the choice claiming no change because the inputs are reversed: the circuit works as drawn. So the answer: the frequency would be lower. Higher is backward.

params.title: A radio needs a steady, tunable frequency

scenes.narration: That oscillator makes a frequency, but not a precise one, and radios need precision. A transmitter must sit exactly on its assigned frequency, and a receiver must tune exactly to it. A simple tunable oscillator can be set anywhere, but it drifts as it warms up. A crystal oscillator, built around a sliver of quartz that vibrates at one precise frequency, is rock steady, but it's fixed on that frequency. We want both: tunable and steady. The trick is to make a tunable oscillator follow a steady reference, called a frequency standard. The circuit that does this is the phase-locked loop. First, let's meet its tunable part.

params.title: The VCO: an oscillator tuned by a voltage

onScreen: Varactor diode: capacitance changes with voltage
Coil and capacitance set the frequency
scenes.narration: Remember resonance: a coil and a capacitor have a natural frequency, and an oscillator built around them runs at that frequency. Change the capacitance, and the frequency changes. A diode is normally a one-way valve for current, but a varactor diode is used for its capacitance, which changes with the voltage across it. Put a varactor in the oscillator's tuned circuit, and now a control voltage sets the frequency. That's a voltage-controlled oscillator, or VCO. Raise or lower the control voltage, and the VCO's frequency follows. All we need now is a circuit that works out the right control voltage, and keeps adjusting it.

blocks.label: Phase detector
blocks.note: Compares the VCO with the reference

blocks.label: Low-pass filter
blocks.note: Smooths the error into a DC voltage

onScreen: Low-pass filter makes a DC control voltage
VCO steered by the control voltage
scenes.narration: Here's that circuit: the phase-locked loop, or PLL. It's a servo loop: a loop that measures its own error and corrects it, like a thermostat. It has 3 parts: a phase detector, a low-pass filter, and the VCO. The phase detector compares the VCO's output with the frequency standard. If the VCO runs even slightly ahead or behind, it produces an error voltage. The low-pass filter passes only slow changes, smoothing that error into a steady DC control voltage. That voltage steers the VCO until it keeps exact step with the reference, cycle for cycle: it's locked. In the exam's words, a PLL is a servo loop consisting of a phase detector, a low-pass filter and a voltage-controlled oscillator.

params.title: Spotting a PLL on the exam
items: Compares a VCO's output with a frequency standard
Its error voltage adjusts a varactor diode's capacitance
That varactor tunes the same VCO: a phase-locked loop
Not a mixer, differential amplifier or plain variable-frequency oscillator
Its parts: phase detector, low-pass filter, VCO. Not a ratio detector

onScreen: Compares a VCO with a frequency standard
Not a mixer, amplifier or plain oscillator
Parts: phase detector, low-pass filter, VCO
scenes.narration: The exam also describes the loop a second way. Picture a circuit that compares the output of a VCO to a frequency standard, and produces an error voltage. That voltage adjusts the capacitance of a varactor diode, the part whose capacitance changes with voltage, and that varactor controls the frequency of that same VCO. That circuit is a phase-locked loop. The other choices don't correct themselves: a mixer combines signals, a differential amplifier amplifies a difference, and a plain variable-frequency oscillator drifts. And for the definition question, the PLL's parts are the phase detector, low-pass filter and VCO: not a ratio detector, a multivibrator or a push-pull amplifier.

params.title: The PLL synthesizer: add a divider

blocks.label: Phase detector
blocks.note: Compares the reference with the divided VCO

blocks.label: Output
blocks.note: A chosen multiple of the reference

blocks.label: VCO
blocks.note: Runs at that many times the reference

onScreen: Output: a multiple of the reference
scenes.narration: A PLL can do more than hold one frequency. Here's the same loop, with one addition. The frequency standard still feeds the phase detector. But now the VCO's output reaches the detector through a frequency divider, a circuit that divides a frequency by a chosen number. The low-pass filter and VCO work as before, and the loop is satisfied only when the divided-down VCO matches the reference. So the output, the VCO itself, runs at that many times the reference frequency. Change the number, and the VCO steps to a new exact frequency, just as steady as the reference. That's a frequency synthesizer: one steady reference, many exact frequencies.

params.title: The PLL synthesizer's impurity
items: Spectrum: the spread of frequencies in a signal
Spectral impurities: unwanted extra signals in it
Exam answer: broadband noise, from the VCO's random phase jitter
Real PLLs also make spurs at discrete frequencies: still pick broadband noise

onScreen: Real PLLs also make spurs; pick broadband noise
scenes.narration: No synthesizer is perfectly clean, though. A signal's spectrum is the spread of frequencies it contains, and any unwanted extra signals in it are called spectral impurities. For the exam, the spectral impurity a phase-locked-loop synthesizer might generate is broadband noise: a hiss spread across a wide range of frequencies on both sides of the wanted signal. It comes from phase noise, the tiny random jitter in the VCO's timing that the loop can't fully correct. Real PLL synthesizers also produce spurs: single unwanted signals at discrete, separate frequencies. But on the exam, choose broadband noise. Digital conversion noise doesn't apply: the VCO makes the signal directly, with no conversion.

blocks.label: Phase comparator
blocks.note: Steps through the wave, tick by tick

blocks.label: DAC
blocks.note: Turns each number into a voltage

blocks.label: Low-pass antialias filter
blocks.note: Smooths the steps into a sine wave

onScreen: Phase comparator steps through the wave
Low-pass antialias filter smooths the steps
scenes.narration: A completely different kind of synthesizer builds the wave from numbers: the direct digital synthesizer, or DDS. Its first part steps through the wave's cycle, one step for every tick of a steady clock signal. The exam calls it a phase comparator. At each step, a look-up table gives the wave's height at that point, from a stored list of values for a sine wave, the smooth wave shape of pure AC. A DAC, a digital-to-analog converter, turns each number into a voltage, making a staircase that follows the sine wave. Finally, a low-pass antialias filter smooths the staircase into a clean wave, removing false copies of the signal, called aliases, that the steps create. So a phase comparator, look-up table, DAC and low-pass antialias filter make a direct digital synthesizer.

params.title: Random noise or regular spurs?
rows: A signal at a definite frequency
A signal at a definite frequency

onScreen: DDS output: spurs at discrete frequencies
scenes.narration: Why do the 2 synthesizers have different impurities? It comes down to the pattern of their errors. The PLL's VCO jitters randomly, and random errors spread out into broadband noise. A DDS makes its errors by rounding. Phase truncation means its position in the wave gets rounded off, and DAC quantization means each voltage is rounded to the nearest step the DAC can make. Those rounding errors repeat in a regular pattern, every time the wave comes round, and a regularly repeating error is itself a signal at a definite frequency. That's why the unwanted components on the output of a direct digital synthesizer are spurs at discrete frequencies, rather than broadband noise.

params.title: The mixer: shifting a signal's frequency

scenes.narration: Our last circuit in this group is the mixer, and it puts an oscillator to work. It takes the incoming RF, or radio frequency, signal from the antenna, and combines it with a signal from the receiver's own oscillator, called the local oscillator. In effect it multiplies the 2 signals, and multiplying 2 waves creates new frequencies: their sum and their difference. Why do that? A receiver converts every station it tunes to one fixed frequency, called the intermediate frequency, or IF, where its filters and amplifiers are designed to work best. So the mixer's output is called the IF output, and later filtering keeps whichever new frequency is wanted.

Let's try the exam's example. A megahertz is a million cycles per second. Feed a mixer an RF input of 200 megahertz and a local oscillator of 150 megahertz. What appears at the IF output before any filtering? The difference: 200 minus 150 is 50 megahertz. The sum: 200 plus 150 is 350 megahertz. And no mixer is perfect, so the original 200 and 150 megahertz signals leak through as well. So the answer is all 4: 50, 150, 200 and 350 megahertz. Choosing only 50, only 350, or just those 2, forgets the signals leaking through.

callouts.label: 3 DC inputs: 100, 200 and 250 mV
Each through its own 10K resistor
All meet at the inverting input (−)
100K feedback resistor, output to the − input; + input grounded
Output: −(R<sub>f</sub>/R<sub>in</sub>) × the sum of the inputs

onScreen: All meet at the inverting input
Output: minus R sub f over R sub in times the sum
scenes.narration: Now for the exam's schematic figures. For each one, name the circuit, then trace what it does. Figure 3D7 should look familiar: it's an inverting amplifier with 3 inputs instead of 1. 3 steady DC voltages, 100, 200 and 250 millivolts, thousandths of a volt, each feed through their own 10 kilohm resistor, and all 3 meet at the inverting input. A 100 kilohm feedback resistor runs from the output back to that same point, and the plus input is grounded. Each input is amplified just as in the inverting amplifier, and their effects add: it's an inverting summing amplifier. So the output is minus R sub f over R sub in, times the sum of the inputs: negative, because the inputs feed the inverting input.

onScreen: V out = minus R sub f over R sub in times the sum
scenes.narration: Let's work out the output. The formula: V out equals minus R sub f over R sub in, times V 1 plus V 2 plus V 3. Step 1, the gain: R sub f over R sub in is 100 kilohms over 10 kilohms, which is 10. Step 2, add the inputs: 100 plus 200 plus 250 millivolts makes 550 millivolts. Step 3, multiply, and keep the minus sign: minus 10 times 550 millivolts. Since 1000 millivolts make 1 volt, that's minus 5.5 volts. Does that make sense? A gain of 10 on a little over half a volt gives a little over 5 volts, inverted, so yes. Plain 5.5 volts forgets the inversion, and 150 millivolts or minus 15 millivolts are far too small for a gain of 10.

params.title: A fault with no figure: the coupling capacitor
items: Amplifier stage: a transistor held ready by steady DC bias voltages
Coupling capacitor: lets the AC signal in, blocks DC
Fails open: the signal can't get in, so no amplification
DC measures normal: the bias never depended on that capacitor

onScreen: Coupling capacitor passes AC, blocks DC
scenes.narration: Not every exam fault comes with a figure: here's one in words. An amplifier stage is usually built around a transistor, a part in which a small current controls a bigger one. It needs steady DC voltages, called its bias, to sit ready, a bit like an engine idling. The AC signal comes in through a coupling capacitor, which passes AC but blocks DC, so the signal gets in without upsetting the bias. What if that capacitor fails open, broken inside like a cut wire? The signal can't reach the amplifier, so no amplification occurs. But the DC within the circuit still measures normal, because the bias never depended on that capacitor. So improper biasing is a trap, and nothing here would cause oscillation or hum.

callouts.label: A series resistor feeds a shunt capacitor
Input jumps up: C charges through R, fast at first, then slower
Input drops: C discharges along the same kind of curve
Answer: output 3, the rounded shark-fin wave

scenes.narration: Capacitors also shape waves. In Figure 3D10, a resistor sits in series, in line with the signal, and a capacitor is connected in shunt, across the output. This is called an integrator. Feed it a square wave, which jumps suddenly between 2 levels. When the input jumps up, the capacitor charges through the resistor: quickly at first, then more and more slowly, because as its voltage rises, less voltage is left across the resistor to push current in. So the output rises along a curve. When the input drops, the capacitor discharges along a similar curve. The result is output 3, the rounded shark-fin wave. Output 1 keeps sharp corners, which this circuit can't make: like the bucket, a capacitor takes time to fill.

params.title: Diodes: one-way valves
items: A diode lets current flow one way only
Symbol: the triangle (anode) points toward the bar (cathode)
Forward biased: anode more positive, it conducts, with about 0.7 V across it
Reverse biased: cathode more positive, it blocks
Tracing + to −: current passes only where the triangle points along the path

onScreen: Triangle is the anode, bar is the cathode
Forward biased: conducts, about 0.7 V across it
Trace from plus to minus, along the triangles
scenes.narration: The next figures use diodes, so here's a quick refresher. A diode is a one-way valve for current. Its symbol is a triangle pointing at a bar. The triangle side is the anode, the bar is the cathode, and the triangle points the way current can flow. When the anode is more positive than the cathode, the diode is forward biased, and it conducts, though a common silicon diode keeps about 0.7 volts across itself while it does. Turn it the other way, with the cathode more positive, and it's reverse biased: it blocks, like a closed valve. On a schematic, we trace current from the positive side of the supply to the negative side, so a diode passes it only if its triangle points along our path.

callouts.label: Trace each path from the battery's positive (top) terminal to its negative
At each diode: does its triangle point along your path?
A lamp lights only through forward-biased diodes
Lit: lamps 2, 3, 4, 7 and 8
Dark: lamps 1, 5, 6 and 9: a reverse-biased diode blocks every path

onScreen: Paths from positive (top) terminal to negative
scenes.narration: Figure 3D8 asks which lamps are lit. A lamp lights only if current can make a complete trip through it, from the battery's positive terminal, at the top, back around to its negative terminal. So for each lamp, trace its paths. At each diode on the way, check that you're travelling the way its triangle points. If a diode points against you, it's reverse biased, and that path is blocked. A lamp is lit if it has at least one path through forward-biased diodes only. Lamps 2, 3, 4, 7 and 8 each have such a path, so they are lit. Lamps 1, 5, 6 and 9 stay dark, because a reverse-biased diode blocks every path through each of them.

Diodes are also at the heart of the next figure, a power supply: the circuit that turns the AC from the wall into the steady DC that electronics need. It works in 4 stages. A transformer, 2 coils sharing a magnetic core, steps the wall voltage down. Rectifier diodes then let current through only one way, turning AC into one-way pulses. With 2 diodes, each handling half of the cycle, both halves get used: that's a full-wave rectifier. A large filter capacitor fills up on each pulse and tops up the gaps between them, smoothing the pulses into fairly steady DC. Finally, a regulator holds the output at a fixed voltage.

params.title: Inside the regulator: the Zener diode

blocks.label: Resistor
blocks.note: Feeds the Zener a small current

blocks.label: Zener diode
blocks.note: Reverse biased: holds its rated voltage

onScreen: A steady reference for the output
scenes.narration: Inside the regulator are 2 more parts. The filtered DC, still not quite steady, feeds a resistor, and the resistor feeds a small current into the first part: a Zener diode. A Zener is a diode made to be used backward, reverse biased. An ordinary diode just blocks in that direction. A Zener blocks too, until the voltage across it reaches its rated value; then it conducts just enough to hold that voltage steady. Think of an overflow drain that keeps a tank at one level: any extra simply runs away. So the Zener's voltage stays put, a steady reference for the output. But a Zener can't carry much current, so it can't power the equipment by itself.

params.title: Inside the regulator: the pass transistor
items: Transistor: 3 connections, base, collector and emitter
A small base current controls a big collector-to-emitter current
2 types, NPN and PNP; in an NPN the collector goes toward the positive side
The Zener holds the base; the emitter follows about 0.7 V below
Pass transistor: the load current passes through it

onScreen: Small base current controls a big one
Emitter about 0.7 V below the base
Pass transistor carries the load current
scenes.narration: That's the job of the second part: a transistor, which you met in the amplifier stage. It has 3 connections: base, collector and emitter. A small current into the base controls a big current from the collector to the emitter: here, the load current, the current the equipment draws. Transistors come in 2 types, NPN and PNP; in an NPN, the collector goes toward the positive side. The Zener holds the base at a steady voltage, and the emitter, which feeds the output, follows about 0.7 volts below it. That's because the base-to-emitter junction behaves like a diode, keeping about 0.7 volts across itself. Wired this way, it's called a pass transistor: the load current passes through it.

callouts.label: D1 and D2: full-wave rectifier, cathodes toward the positive line
C1: filter capacitor
R1 feeds D3, the 9.1 V Zener
D3 holds the base of TR1 steady
TR1: NPN pass transistor, emitter to the output
Answer: there is no problem with the circuit

onScreen: R1 feeds the 9.1 V Zener D3
scenes.narration: Now Figure 3D9. The exam asks whether anything is wrong with this regulated power supply, so let's name the parts. The top wire is the positive line. D1 and D2 form the full-wave rectifier, with their cathodes toward the positive line. That's right for a positive supply, because current leaves a diode through its cathode. C1 is the filter capacitor. R1 feeds D3, the 9.1 volt Zener diode, and D3 holds the base of TR1 steady. TR1 is the NPN pass transistor, with its collector on the positive line and its emitter feeding the output. Every part is where it belongs, so the answer is: there is no problem with the circuit.

params.title: Figure 3D9: the output voltage
steps: The Zener holds TR1's base at 9.1 V
The emitter sits about 0.7 V lower

onScreen: V out about V Zener minus 0.7 V
scenes.narration: Let's check the output voltage, to be sure the supply does its job. The Zener holds TR1's base at 9.1 volts. The emitter, which feeds the output, follows about 0.7 volts below the base. So the output is 9.1 minus 0.7: about 8.4 volts. That's the nominal 9 volts marked on the drawing; nominal means the round figure it's named for. So nothing needs changing. Don't believe the choices that find a fault: D1 and D2 are not reversed, R1 is not too low, and TR1 does not need to be a PNP, since an NPN with its collector on the positive line is exactly right.

callouts.label: Series resistor, then a shunt diode across the output
The diode's anode faces the output line
Positive half-cycles: the diode conducts, output clipped at about +0.7 V
Negative half-cycles: the diode blocks, the full swing passes
Answer: output waveform 2

onScreen: Positive half-cycles clipped at about +0.7 V
scenes.narration: One last figure, and it uses that 0.7 volts again. Figure 3D11 has a series resistor feeding a shunt diode across the output, with the diode's anode facing the output line. Feed it pure AC, a plain sine wave. On each positive half-cycle, the output line goes positive, which forward biases the diode. It conducts, and holds the output at about plus 0.7 volts, clipping off the top, while the rest of the voltage appears across the series resistor. On each negative half-cycle, the diode is reverse biased and blocks, so the full negative swing passes. That's output waveform 2. Output 1 is the untouched sine wave, and output 3 is the mirror image you'd get with the diode turned around.

params.title: Key facts to remember
items: Resonance: series impedance ≈ R, minimum, current maximum; parallel ≈ R, maximum
Op-amps: gain set by external feedback to the − input; inverting: 180°; comparator: open loop
PLL: phase detector, low-pass filter, VCO. Exam impurity: broadband noise; DDS: spurs
Mixer: sum, difference and both inputs: 50, 150, 200 and 350 MHz
Figures: 3D7 gives −5.5 V; 3D9 has no problem; a conducting diode drops about 0.7 V

onScreen: Op-amp feedback; inverting 180°; comparator open loop
PLL parts; broadband noise; DDS spurs
scenes.narration: To wrap up, 5 things to remember. First, resonance: X sub L equals X sub C. In series, the impedance is about the resistance, its minimum, so the current is maximum; in parallel, it's about the resistance, its maximum. Second, op-amps: external feedback, from the output to the inverting input, sets the gain; an inverting amplifier's output is 180 degrees out of phase; and a comparator runs open-loop. Third, a PLL is a phase detector, low-pass filter and VCO; for the exam its impurity is broadband noise, while a DDS makes discrete spurs. Fourth, a mixer gives the sum, the difference and both originals: 50, 150, 200 and 350 megahertz. Last, the figures: minus 5.5 volts, no problem with the power supply, and about 0.7 volts across a conducting diode.
